name: Bianca Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pedro and I rent Highgate Farm from the Ashcombe estate, 160 hectares on the hill. We run 600 breeding ewes and grow seed potatoes and a bit of barley. I'm out at six with the dogs to check the ewes, then it's whatever's broken, and there's always something broken. I've got one shepherd, Walter, who's 66 and better on a hillside than men half his age.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like lambing, and I like grading seed potatoes, believe it or not, because I'm good at it and buyers know my name. What wears me out is the estate's land agent, a young man with a clipboard who's never lambed a ewe. Our tenancy is up for renewal in 2028, and he's been dropping hints about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop talking about it. I don't use any of that AI stuff and I don't miss it. At the market I'd say the same: sheep don't care about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never my worry. My worry is the rent review in 2028 and whether the estate wants us gone. A computer never kept me awake, but the estate's land agent has, more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what we do, same flock, same potato buyer. I'd trim the extras, like the new quad bike Pedro's been eyeing, and keep our four months of savings for the rent review. I'd also get our accountant to put our figures in order before the agent asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, just because farming on someone else's land always feels a bit borrowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the rent goes up a lot in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the flock, maybe to 450, and let Walter go part-time, which would break my heart. Or we'd give up the tenancy. At 60 that's not a fresh start, that's an ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Pedro say about giving up the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pedro would say we've done our bit and his job at the feed mill would carry us. He's more relaxed than me. But I've been on this hill thirty-one years, and I'm not ready to hand back the keys.

say: Good, now we can **stop talking** about AI.
Sheep **don't care** about computers, and neither do I.
I'd say the same at the **market** to anyone who asked.
think: AI was never my worry; the **2028 rent review** is.
Farming **rented land** always feels a bit borrowed and insecure.
do: Shelve the **new quad bike** Pedro wants.
Keep **four months of savings** ready for the rent review.
Ask the accountant to **tidy the figures** before the land agent asks.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the tenancy makes the farm feel **borrowed**.
S0.quote: A computer never kept me awake, but the estate's land agent has, more than once.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **tenancy and rent**, which AI doesn't touch either way.
She would sooner **shrink the flock** than give up, but hates letting Walter go.
Her husband is the **calmer partner**, with a steady wage at the feed mill.

steps.text: Shelve the new quad bike and hold savings for the rent review
Keep the same 600-ewe flock and the same seed potato buyer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices but it won't lamb a ewe. At the market I'd tell people not to be bullied into buying software they don't need. I wouldn't post anything online, I'm not on there much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me because the estate would love it. The land agent could use software to work out exactly how much rent he can squeeze, and the estate might decide to farm the land itself with a contractor and a computer. Tenants like Pedro and me are the first thing an estate cuts when software says it can do the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get our daughter Marta, who's an accountant, to go through our costs and build the best case for keeping the tenancy. I'd cut the flock to 500 and drop the barley if the rent goes up. I wouldn't buy any AI myself, but I'd let Marta use it on our numbers if she wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like watching the agent sharpen his pencil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Marta use AI on your numbers but you wouldn't. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta knows what it's doing and I don't. I'm too old to learn a new trick that might be gone in two years. She can do it, and I'll check it against what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else on the hill would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter, for sure, he's 66 and he won't retire. And the young couple at Brook End, who've borrowed for a new shed. If the estate gets clever with software, they'll be squeezed before we are.

say: It's fine for offices, but it **won't lamb a ewe**.
Farmers shouldn't be **bullied into buying** software they don't need.
think: The **estate** would use AI to squeeze rent or farm the land itself.
**Tenants** are the first cut when software can do the sums.
do: Ask Marta to build the **best case** for keeping the tenancy.
Cut the flock to **500 ewes** and drop barley if rent rises.
Let Marta use AI on the **farm accounts** while she checks the results.
feel: **Anxious**, like watching the land agent **sharpen his pencil**.
S1.quote: Tenants like Pedro and me are the first thing an estate cuts when software says it can do the sums.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **tool for the landlord**, not for her.
She is willing to let **her daughter** use AI on her behalf but won't touch it.
Her concern widens to **other tenants** and her elderly shepherd.

steps.text: Ask Marta to build a cost case for keeping the tenancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to protect tenant farmers, and fast. At the market I'd say whoever owns the land owns the future now. I'd probably sign a petition, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd lose Highgate. The planning and paperwork goes to AI in 2028, the same year as our rent review, and the estate would want a robot operation by 2031. I'd be 63, with a shepherd's crook and no farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit with Marta and Pedro and work out if we can live on Pedro's mill wage plus savings. I'd stop all spending on the farm except feed and vet bills. I'd sell 200 ewes in the autumn sale to raise cash, and I'd ask the estate for a five-year lease before the agent knows what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a storm coming up the valley and the sheep still on the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between the thinking AI and the robots mean for your farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing good. The estate gets the brains in 2028 and starts planning without us, and then in 2031 the robot shepherds come. Three years is just long enough for them to show us the door politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Walter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the truth, over a pint at the Plough. He'd say he's seen worse, he always does. But I don't think he has.

say: The government must **protect tenant farmers** now.
Whoever **owns the land** owns the future now.
I'd **sign a petition** for tenants, which I've never done before.
think: We'd likely **lose Highgate**, with the rent review landing in 2028.
The estate would plan for a **robot operation** by 2031.
do: Stop all **farm spending** except feed and vet bills.
Sell **200 ewes** in the autumn sale to raise cash.
Ask the estate for a **five-year lease** before the agent catches on.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a storm coming with the sheep still on the top.
S2.quote: I'd be 63, with a shepherd's crook and no farm.
fieldNote: The AI date collides with her **rent review**, which doubles the threat.
She expects to **lose the farm** and her livelihood, not just change her work.
For a resistant person she moves fast: **selling stock** and seeking a lease.

steps.text: Sell 200 ewes in the autumn sale to raise cash
Stop all farm spending except feed and vet bills
Ask the estate for a five-year lease straight away
Sign a petition for tenant farmer protection

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to argue our case. At the tenants' association I'd push for longer leases in law. To friends I'd say get your paperwork straight now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still bad but survivable. We'd get through the 2028 rent review before AI is everywhere, and robots wouldn't reach the hill till 2034. By 2034 I'd be 66, which is about when Pedro and I would hand back the keys anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fight hard for a long lease in 2028, at least seven years. I'd join the tenants' association, which I've always said I'd do. And I'd put 100 a month extra into savings and keep the flock as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It's a hard climb, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about how you farm in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe let Marta set up some of that software for ordering feed, if the other farms prove it works. I'm not going to be the first, I never am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen to Highgate when you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a young family on it, not a robot company. That's the bit I'd fight for. I'd tell the estate that to their faces.

Tenants need **longer leases** written into law.
Get your **paperwork straight** now, while there's time.
think: It's **bad but survivable**, since robots won't reach the hill till 2034.
At 66, we'd **hand back the keys** around then anyway.
do: Fight for a **seven-year lease** at the 2028 review.
Add **100 a month** to savings and keep the flock steady.
feel: **Anxious** but able to breathe; a **hard climb**, not a cliff.
S3.quote: By 2034 I'd be 66, which is about when Pedro and I would hand back the keys anyway.
fieldNote: The extra years let the robots arrive near her **natural retirement**.
Her fight shifts to **who farms Highgate next**: a young family, not a firm.
She'd follow others on software, **never first**.

steps.text: Negotiate at least a seven-year lease at the 2028 review
Join the tenants' association and push for longer leases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone sensible to plan. At the market I'd say this one's for the young ones to sort out. I'd probably just shrug, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be retired before the robots come. I'm 68 when the AI arrives and 71 for the robots, and Pedro and I plan to stop at 65. My worry in a slow world is the next tenant on our hill, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd farm on to 65 the way I do now. I'd get a decent lease in 2028 and use the years to hand the flock to a younger shepherd, maybe through the estate's starter scheme. We'd save a bit extra for the retirement cottage in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the hill, calm for myself. Mostly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Luis about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis is a police officer, and I'd tell him people will always need policing by people. Then I'd tell him to come and help with the lambing while there's still lambing to help with. He'd laugh, but he'd come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss if a robot did your job one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smell of the lambing shed at four in the morning. A robot can't miss that, can it?

say: Ten years is **enough to plan** for anyone sensible.
This one's for the **young ones** to sort out.
think: I'd be **retired** before the robots arrive in 2039.
My worry is the **next tenant** on our hill, not me.
Pedro and I plan to **stop at 65** anyway.
do: Farm on to **65** exactly as now.
Secure a **decent lease** in 2028 and train a younger shepherd.
Save a little extra for a **retirement cottage** in the village.
feel: **Calm** for herself, **uneasy** for the hill and its future.
S4.quote: My worry in a slow world is the next tenant on our hill, not me.
fieldNote: Ten years makes the robots a **next-generation** problem for her.
Her lingering unease is the **tenancy** and who comes after.

steps.text: Farm the flock and potatoes as now until 65

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands on our rent review and gives the estate every reason to push us off. What would help is a law that gives tenants first right to stay on, and a long lease, before landlords can bring in robot contractors. And somebody explaining it in plain words, not on a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land. People talk about robots taking jobs, but on this hill the robot would just be the estate's new tenant.

headlineQuote: People talk about robots taking jobs, but on this hill the robot would just be the estate's new tenant.
portrait: Bianca, 58, rents a **hill farm** with 600 ewes and seed potatoes from a big estate.
She **never uses AI** and lets her accountant daughter handle anything digital.
Her real pressure is a **2028 rent review** and a land agent she distrusts.
In fast scenarios she expects to **lose the farm**; with more time, retirement arrives first.
Pragmatic and centrist, she wants **tenant protection** rather than help for herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands on her rent review and pushes the estate toward robots.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving tenants **first right** to stay on with a **long lease**.
**Plain explanations** in person, not on a website.
